title: When everything feels urgent: sort it, then act
performance: given a list of competing work requests, the viewer can place each by impact and effort, do the quick wins first, schedule the big ones, and decline or defer the rest with a reasoned sentence

audience.assumed_prior: knows their own job and tools; feels overloaded; has no simple sorting method
audience.why: corporate employees, general audience, no prerequisite
audience.motivation: wants to stop working in arrival order and stop letting important work slip
audience.context: desktop or phone, sound on, short break between tasks

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: one person's real-feeling Monday list carries every idea; the matrix is only named once the tasks have landed on the board
strategy.signature_move: place a task from the running list on the board, act on it, THEN name the zone and the rule just used

misconceptions.belief: the request that feels most urgent is the most important one
misconceptions.why_tempting: deadlines and pings are loud; research on the mere urgency effect suggests we lean toward the nearer deadline

misconceptions.belief: saying no to a colleague or manager is just refusing
misconceptions.why_tempting: it feels like letting someone down

hook.sketch: Monday, four requests, every one flagged urgent; she starts at the top of the inbox.

arc.promise: two questions per task turn the pile into an order you can defend
arc.bridge_from_prior: from the inbox order the viewer already works in, to an order chosen on purpose

sections.goal: the viewer can classify a task by impact and effort and explain why urgency is a separate question
sections.carrier: the board: two axes drawn, tasks placed as notes

sections.goal: the viewer can use a task's zone to pick its action: quick wins now, major projects scheduled in a block, fill-ins batched, thankless tasks declined
sections.carrier: the same board, zones named and actions written beside them

sections.goal: the viewer can use a reply that ties a no or later to a priority and offers a concrete alternative
concepts: later with a date or trade
sections.carrier: a reply drafted beside the board

arc.payoff: a new request lands; the viewer places it before the narrator does; the opening list now stands in order, with the habit of re-sorting when work arrives (F14)

practice_ladder.what: the four Monday tasks placed and acted on, every step narrated
the meeting invite with no purpose: zone given, the viewer hears the reply shape
a new request from her manager arrives; the viewer places it before the reveal

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Her manager asks for a big new analysis by Friday. Where does it go, and what does she say?
recall_moments.answer: high impact, high effort: schedule it in a block and ask which existing task gives way
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: do it right now because it is urgent and from the manager

transfer_tasks: before starting tomorrow, put your next three requests on the two questions and do one quick win first

persona.voice: a capable colleague talking a peer through their own Monday, calm and a little wry about the urgent label
persona.delivery_notes: brisk on the setup, slower on the four actions, warm on saying no

gagne.objective: promise: an order you can defend
gagne.recall_prior: the inbox order the viewer already uses
gagne.present: board built in dependency order: axes, tasks, zones, actions, reply
gagne.guidance: signature move on each Monday task
gagne.practice: faded reply in sec3; quiz after sec3
gagne.feedback: quiz answer explained with the tempting wrong
gagne.assess: viewer places the new request first

merrill.problem_centered: her Monday list is the running problem
merrill.demonstration: each task placed before the zone is named
merrill.application: the manager's request in the check

mayer.signalling: one slowdown on the four actions
mayer.redundancy: board shows short labels only; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each note lands as it is named
mayer.pre_training: impact and effort named before the zones
